scenarios.title: Taking Turns
scenarios.summary: Learn how to take turns and share toys with friends.

phases.title: Taking Turns with Toys
phases.prompt: Do you like playing with toys? I love toys too! If we both want to play with the same toy, what should we do?

choices.text: Take the toy from my friend.
choices.feedback: If we take the toy without asking, our friend might feel sad. Let's try asking first.

choices.text: Ask, "Can I have a turn, please?"
choices.feedback: Great job! Asking nicely helps friends want to share. Sometimes they say "no", and that is okay. We can wait for our turn.

choices.text: Walk away and say nothing.
choices.feedback: Walking away is okay. If you really want to play, you can try asking first. Maybe your friend will share.

phases.title: Trading Toys
phases.prompt: My friend is playing with a toy I like. I have a different toy. What can I do?

choices.text: Grab the toy from my friend.
choices.feedback: If we grab a toy, our friend might feel upset. Let's try offering a trade instead.

choices.text: Offer to trade my toy for theirs.
choices.feedback: That is so kind! Trading is a great way to share. Now you both have something fun.

choices.text: Get upset and walk away.
choices.feedback: It is hard when you really want a toy. You can ask, "Do you want to trade?" Then you both can be happy.

phases.title: Using a Timer
phases.prompt: Someone else is already using the toy. We could use a timer so everyone gets a turn. What should I do?

choices.text: Use a timer and wait for my turn.
choices.feedback: Great job! A timer makes turns fair. When the timer beeps, it is your turn.

choices.text: Keep asking my friend again and again.
choices.feedback: Asking many times can make our friend feel stressed. A timer helps everyone know when it is their turn.

choices.text: Get upset and leave.
choices.feedback: Waiting is hard. A timer shows us exactly how long to wait. Let's give it a try.

phases.title: Waiting for My Turn
phases.prompt: My friend is not ready to share yet, and that is okay. What can I do while I wait?

choices.text: Ask my friend to tell me when they are done, and play with something else.
choices.feedback: Smart choice! Now you can play with something else while you wait.

choices.text: Take the toy anyway.
choices.feedback: Taking the toy might make our friend sad. Let's ask them to tell us when they are done.

choices.text: Stand still and feel upset.
choices.feedback: It is okay to feel upset. Waiting can be tough. You can ask your friend when they will be done, and find something else to do.

phases.title: Asking an Adult for Help
phases.prompt: We tried asking, trading, and waiting, but it still does not feel fair. What can I do?

choices.text: Ask a teacher or parent for help.
choices.feedback: Great choice! Adults can help make sure everyone gets a turn.

choices.text: Yell at my friend.
choices.feedback: Yelling can make things harder. Let's try asking an adult to help instead.

choices.text: Give up and walk away.
choices.feedback: Taking a break is okay. You can also ask an adult for help. That is what they are there for.

phases.title: Celebrating Good Choices
phases.prompt: You learned so much about taking turns! You can ask, trade, use a timer, wait, or ask an adult. Are you ready to play with friends?

choices.text: I am ready to play with friends!
choices.feedback: Fantastic! You know all about taking turns now.

scenarios.title: Saying Hello
scenarios.summary: Practice greeting someone new at school.

phases.title: Someone New
phases.prompt: There is a new kid in class today. They are sitting by themselves. What could I do?

choices.text: Walk over and say hello.
choices.feedback: Nice! Saying hello is a friendly way to help someone feel welcome.

choices.text: Stay in my seat and say nothing.
choices.feedback: That is okay if you are not ready. When you feel ready, a small wave or "hi" can help a new kid feel welcome.

choices.text: Run over and give them a big hug.
choices.feedback: Hugs are for people we know well, and we ask first. With someone new, a wave or "hello" is better.

phases.title: How to Say Hi
phases.prompt: I am standing near the new kid. Which way of saying hello is friendly?

choices.text: Say "Hi, I'm" and my name in a calm voice.
choices.feedback: Great! You can look at their face or near them, whatever feels comfortable for you.

choices.text: Shout "HELLO!" really loudly.
choices.feedback: A loud voice can be a surprise. An inside voice is easier for people to hear comfortably.

choices.text: Smile and wave.
choices.feedback: A wave is a great way to say hi without words!

phases.title: Asking Their Name
phases.prompt: The new kid waves back. What can I say next?

choices.text: Ask, "What's your name?"
choices.feedback: Good question! Learning someone's name is a great way to start being friends.

choices.text: Talk for a long time about my favorite dinosaurs.
choices.feedback: Sharing what you love is great! First, ask their name. Then you can ask, "Do you like dinosaurs?"

choices.text: Walk away without saying anything.
choices.feedback: They might wonder where you went. You can say "What's your name?" or "Bye, see you later!"

phases.title: When They Are Quiet
phases.prompt: I asked their name, but they did not answer right away. Maybe they feel shy. What can I do?

choices.text: Wait a little and give them time.
choices.feedback: Great patience! Some people need more time to answer. That is okay.

choices.text: Ask again louder and louder.
choices.feedback: A louder voice can make a shy person feel more nervous. Try waiting a little instead.

choices.text: Say, "That's okay. See you later!"
choices.feedback: Kind words! You let them know it is okay, and you can try again another time.

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: You know how to say hello! Walk over, say hi or wave, ask their name, and give them time.

choices.text: I can say hello!
choices.feedback: Wonderful! Saying hello is the first step to making a friend.

scenarios.title: Joining a Game
scenarios.summary: Learn how to ask to play with other kids at recess.

phases.title: At Recess
phases.prompt: Some kids are playing ball at recess. I want to play too. What should I do first?

choices.text: Watch for a minute to learn the game.
choices.feedback: Smart! Watching first helps you learn the rules before you join.

choices.text: Run in and grab the ball.
choices.feedback: The other kids might be surprised. Let's watch first, then ask to join.

choices.text: Stand far away and hope they ask me.
choices.feedback: They might not know you want to play. You can walk closer and ask them.

phases.title: Asking to Play
phases.prompt: There is a break in the game. What can I say?

choices.text: Ask, "Can I play too?"
choices.feedback: Great asking! A short, friendly question is a great way to join.

choices.text: Say, "You're playing it wrong. Here are the real rules."
choices.feedback: Every group can have its own rules. Ask to join first, and play their way.

choices.text: Stand in the middle of the game without asking.
choices.feedback: Standing in the game can get in the way. Asking "Can I play?" lets everyone know.

phases.title: If They Say "Not Now"
phases.prompt: One kid says, "Not right now, the teams are full." I feel disappointed. What can I do?

choices.text: Say "Okay" and find something else to do, or ask to play next game.
choices.feedback: That is a calm, flexible choice! You can ask again later, or play something else.

choices.text: Yell, "That's not fair!"
choices.feedback: Feeling disappointed is okay. Yelling can make it harder. Try "Okay, can I play next time?"

choices.text: Ask a teacher to help me find a game.
choices.feedback: Good idea! Teachers can help you find a game to join.

phases.title: Playing Together
phases.prompt: The next game starts and they say, "You can play now!" During the game, what is a friendly thing to do?

choices.text: Follow the rules and pass the ball to others.
choices.feedback: Great teamwork! Passing and following rules makes the game fun for everyone.

choices.text: Keep the ball the whole time.
choices.feedback: Other kids want a turn too. Passing the ball helps everyone have fun.

choices.text: Say "Nice try!" when someone misses.
choices.feedback: So kind! Encouraging words help friends feel good.

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: You know how to join a game! Watch first, ask "Can I play?", stay calm if they say "not now", and share the ball.

choices.text: I can join a game!
choices.feedback: Awesome! Have fun playing with friends.

scenarios.title: When Plans Change
scenarios.summary: Practice what to do when something unexpected happens.

phases.title: Unexpected News
phases.prompt: We were going to the park today. Now it is raining, so we cannot go. I feel upset. What can I do first?

choices.text: Say how I feel: "I feel disappointed."
choices.feedback: Great job using words! Naming your feeling helps grown-ups understand and help you.

choices.text: Throw my things on the floor.
choices.feedback: Big feelings are okay. Throwing things can break them or hurt someone. Let's use words or take a breath.

choices.text: Go to my calm spot for a minute.
choices.feedback: Good choice! A calm spot can help your body feel better.

phases.title: Calming My Body
phases.prompt: My body still feels tight and hot. What can help me calm down?

choices.text: Take slow breaths, like blowing up a balloon.
choices.feedback: Breathe in slowly... and out slowly. Slow breaths help your body feel calm.

choices.text: Squeeze my hands or hug a pillow.
choices.feedback: Squeezing can help your body feel calmer. That is a great tool.

choices.text: Keep thinking about how unfair it is.
choices.feedback: It is okay to feel that way. Let's try a calming tool first, like slow breaths.

phases.title: Asking What Happens Next
phases.prompt: I feel a little calmer. I want to know what will happen instead. What can I do?

choices.text: Ask, "What are we going to do instead?"
choices.feedback: Great question! Knowing the new plan can make change feel less scary.

choices.text: Ask, "Can we go to the park another day?"
choices.feedback: Good thinking! Sometimes plans can move to a new day.

choices.text: Cover my ears and not listen.
choices.feedback: Covering ears can help when things are loud. When you are ready, listening to the new plan can help you feel better.

phases.title: Trying the New Plan
phases.prompt: The new plan is to build a puzzle and bake cookies at home. What can I do?

choices.text: Give the new plan a try.
choices.feedback: That is being flexible! New plans can be fun too.

choices.text: Say "No" to everything.
choices.feedback: It is okay to still feel disappointed. You can choose one thing from the new plan to try.

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: When plans change you can say how you feel, calm your body, ask what happens next, and try the new plan.

choices.text: I can handle changes!
choices.feedback: Wonderful! Being flexible is a super skill.

scenarios.title: Too Loud!
scenarios.summary: Learn what to do when a place feels too loud or busy.

phases.title: A Noisy Room
phases.prompt: The lunchroom is very loud. My body feels uncomfortable and my ears hurt. That is a real feeling. What can I do?

choices.text: Put on my headphones or cover my ears.
choices.feedback: Great choice! Headphones or covering your ears can make the noise smaller.

choices.text: Run out of the room without telling anyone.
choices.feedback: It makes sense to want to get away. Adults need to know where you are so you stay safe. Let's tell an adult first.

choices.text: Stay and try to ignore it.
choices.feedback: You are trying very hard! You do not have to just put up with it. There are tools that can help.

phases.title: Telling an Adult
phases.prompt: It is still too loud. How can I let an adult know I need help?

choices.text: Say, "It's too loud. I need a break."
choices.feedback: Great job! Telling an adult helps them help you.

choices.text: Show my break card.
choices.feedback: Perfect! A break card is a great way to ask without words.

choices.text: Scream so they notice me.
choices.feedback: Screaming can make the room even louder. Try words or a break card instead.

phases.title: Taking a Break
phases.prompt: My teacher says I can go to the quiet corner. What can I do there?

choices.text: Take slow breaths.
choices.feedback: Slow breaths help your body feel calm again.

choices.text: Use my fidget, rock, or move in a way that helps me.
choices.feedback: Moving your body in ways that feel good is a great calming tool.

choices.text: Look at a favorite book quietly.
choices.feedback: A quiet activity can help you feel calm.

phases.title: Feeling Ready
phases.prompt: I feel calm now. What can I do next?

choices.text: Tell my teacher, "I'm ready," and go back with my headphones.
choices.feedback: Great job! You used your tools and came back when you were ready.

choices.text: Ask for a little more time if I need it.
choices.feedback: That is okay! Knowing when you need more time is an important skill.

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: When it is too loud, you can use headphones, tell an adult, take a break, and go back when you are ready.

choices.text: I know what to do when it is too loud!
choices.feedback: Wonderful! Taking care of your body is very important.

scenarios.title: Losing a Game
scenarios.summary: Practice being a good sport when you don't win.

phases.title: The Game Is Over
phases.prompt: I was playing a board game with my friend. My friend won. I feel frustrated. What can I do?

choices.text: Take a deep breath.
choices.feedback: Great! A deep breath helps your body feel calmer when you are frustrated.

choices.text: Knock the game pieces off the table.
choices.feedback: Losing can feel really bad. Knocking pieces off can upset your friend. Try a deep breath first.

choices.text: Cry.
choices.feedback: It is okay to cry when you feel sad. When you are ready, you can take a deep breath.

phases.title: What to Say
phases.prompt: I feel a little calmer. What can I say to my friend?

choices.text: Say, "Good game!"
choices.feedback: That is being a good sport! Your friend will want to play again.

choices.text: Say, "You cheated!"
choices.feedback: Saying "You cheated" can hurt feelings when it is not true. Try "Good game!"

choices.text: Ask, "Can we play again?"
choices.feedback: Great idea! Playing again is a fun way to keep practicing.

phases.title: Win or Lose
phases.prompt: We play again and this time I win! What can I do?

choices.text: Say, "Good game, thanks for playing!"
choices.feedback: Perfect! Good sports are kind when they win and when they lose.

choices.text: Say, "Ha ha, you lost!"
choices.feedback: Teasing can make your friend feel sad, the way you felt before. Try "Good game!"

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: Games are for fun. Win or lose, you can take a breath and say "Good game!"

choices.text: I can be a good sport!
choices.feedback: Wonderful! Your friends will love playing with you.

scenarios.title: Asking for Help
scenarios.summary: Learn how to ask a teacher for help in class.

phases.title: I'm Stuck
phases.prompt: I am doing my worksheet in class. I do not understand question 3. What can I do?

choices.text: Raise my hand.
choices.feedback: Great job! Raising your hand tells the teacher you need help.

choices.text: Crumple up the paper.
choices.feedback: Feeling stuck is frustrating. Crumpling the paper means you lose your work. Let's ask for help instead.

choices.text: Call out, "I don't get it!"
choices.feedback: Using words is good! In class, raising your hand first helps the teacher hear everyone.

phases.title: Waiting for the Teacher
phases.prompt: My teacher is helping another student. She says, "I'll be there in a minute." What can I do?

choices.text: Put my hand down and wait.
choices.feedback: Great waiting! Your teacher knows you need help and is coming.

choices.text: Work on a question I do know while I wait.
choices.feedback: Smart! Doing a different question uses your waiting time well.

choices.text: Keep saying, "Teacher! Teacher!"
choices.feedback: Your teacher already heard you. Let's wait quietly for her to come.

phases.title: Saying What I Need
phases.prompt: My teacher comes over and asks, "How can I help?" What can I say?

choices.text: Point to it and say, "I don't understand number 3."
choices.feedback: Perfect! Telling exactly what you need helps your teacher help you fast.

choices.text: Say, "I don't know."
choices.feedback: That is a start! Pointing to the part you are stuck on helps your teacher know what to explain.

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: Everyone needs help sometimes. Raise your hand, wait, and say what you need.

choices.text: I can ask for help!
choices.feedback: Great job! Asking for help is a brave and smart thing to do.

scenarios.title: Personal Space
scenarios.summary: Learn about giving people room and asking before touching.

phases.title: Standing in Line
phases.prompt: We are lining up for lunch. Everyone has a little bubble of space around them. Where should I stand?

choices.text: About one arm's length behind the person in front.
choices.feedback: Great job! One arm's length gives everyone room to feel comfortable.

choices.text: Right up close, touching their back.
choices.feedback: Being very close can make people feel squished. Try standing one arm's length away.

phases.title: Asking Before Hugs
phases.prompt: I am happy to see my friend and I want to give them a hug. What should I do?

choices.text: Ask, "Can I give you a hug?"
choices.feedback: Wonderful! Asking first shows you care about how your friend feels.

choices.text: Hug them without asking.
choices.feedback: Some people do not like surprise hugs. Asking first helps everyone feel safe.

phases.title: When Someone Says No
phases.prompt: My friend says, "No thanks, I don't want a hug." What can I do?

choices.text: Say "Okay!" and give a high five or wave instead.
choices.feedback: Great! Respecting "no" is what good friends do. A wave is a fun way to say hi.

choices.text: Hug them anyway.
choices.feedback: When someone says no, we listen. Everyone gets to decide about their own body, including you.

choices.text: Feel sad and think they do not like me.
choices.feedback: It is okay to feel a little sad. Saying no to a hug does not mean they do not like you. They just want space.

phases.title: You Did It!
phases.prompt: Give people an arm's length of space, ask before hugs, and listen when someone says no.

choices.text: I know about personal space!
choices.feedback: Fantastic! Respecting space helps everyone feel comfortable.
